newsitem.title: TANZANIA: African leaders give Burundi an ultimatum.
newsitem.headline: African leaders give Burundi an ultimatum.

text.p: African leaders told Burundi's military ruler Pierre Buyoya on Saturday to open unconditional talks with Hutu rebels within a month or face further sanctions.

Defying a U.S. suggestion to ease the embargo, now more than two months old, the regional leaders said they would send a team to Burundi to check on Buyoya's commitment to unconditional negotiations stated in a letter from him to the Arusha summit meeting.

"The summit reiterated that the objective of the sanctions is to serve as an effective means of securing a negotiated settlement between all parties to the conflict," they said after nearly six hours of talks.

"The summit agreed to appoint a ministerial committee made up of Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, Tanzania and Cameroon to visit Burundi to ascertain Buyoya's committment to unconditional negotiations with other groups," they said in a final statement.
Buyoya had previously agreed to peace talks in principle but he and the rebels had not agreed to each other's preconditions.
The leaders said they had a letter from Buyoya committing himself to unconditional talks with the Hutu National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD) and other Hutu rebel groups.
In Brussels, CNDD spokesman Jerome Ndiho told Reuters CNDD was willing to talk to Buyoya, but only as leader of the army.
"We will talk with Buyoya as the main leader of the army because it is the army which is killing people," said Ndiho, adding that the Hutu rebels had demanded talks for two years.
He said CNDD still demanded Buyoya stand down as president because it could not negotiate with the man it blamed for the killing of Hutu president Melchior Ndadaye by soldiers in 1993.

Ethnic war between Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army and Hutu rebels is killing up to 1,000 people monthly and regional leaders fear the country could go down the same path as Rwanda where up to a million people were killed in genocide in 1994.
"Non-compliance or obstruction of the negotiation process will lead to additional measures being taken against the regime and any of the factions," the African leaders warned Buyoya.

But dangling the prospect of rewards for talks in front of Buyoya's military-appointed government, they added: "The summit also undertook to further respond positively should the regime enter into negotiation with all parties to the conflict."

Officials said Ethiopia, which has close ties to Washington, and Rwanda, considered the weakest link in sanctions because of ethnic sympathies, both suggested easing the embargo imposed in revenge for Buyoya seizing power in an army coup on July 25.
But others, led by Tanzania, Kenya and Zambia, argued giving way would only be rewarding Buyoya before he even began talks.
Reflecting their displeasure with Buyoya for using the army to oust civilian president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, the leaders met without him despite his request to be invited as head of state.

U.S. officials said U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher made clear on Friday to East African leaders in Arusha the U.S. view that Buyoya had taken some positive steps by lifting bans on parliament and political parties in Burundi.
"The secretary in his discussions said, and others agreed, that there should be some effort to acknowledge progress when and as it is made," said a U.S. official with Christopher.
The summit consisted of the presidents of Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda, Tanzania, Zambia, the prime ministers of Ethiopia and Zaire and the secretary-general of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU).
Also attending the one-day talks were representatives of the United States and the European Union and former Tanzanian president Julius Nyerere, international mediator on Burundi.
